questions.question: What is dependency scope in Maven and what are the main scope values?
questions.title: Maven Dependency Scopes
questions.direct_answer: Dependency scope controls when a dependency is available on the classpath: 'compile' (always, default), 'test' (test classes only), 'runtime' (runtime only, not compile), and 'provided' (at compile time, but provided by the container at runtime).

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Maven dependency management knowledge — scopes prevent classpath bloat and make intentions explicit
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting everything in compile scope by default — JUnit should always be test scope
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give concrete examples: JUnit → test, JDBC driver → runtime, servlet-api → provided

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Dependency scope tells Maven when a dependency should be on the classpath and whether it gets included in the packaged artifact. The four main scopes are: 'compile' is the default — the dependency is on the classpath at compile time, test time, and runtime, and it's included in the JAR or WAR. Most of your Spring, Jackson, and Guava dependencies use compile scope. 'test' means the dependency is only on the classpath during test compilation and execution — it's not included in the packaged artifact. JUnit, Mockito, and H2 (in-memory test DB) should always be test scope. 'runtime' means the dependency isn't needed at compile time (you don't reference it directly in source code) but is needed at runtime. The classic example is JDBC drivers — your code compiles against the java.sql interface, not the specific driver, so the driver is only needed at runtime. 'provided' means you need the dependency at compile time but it won't be in the packaged artifact because the deployment container provides it — like the servlet API when deploying a WAR to Tomcat: Tomcat provides the servlet API, so you don't include it in the WAR.

sections.title: Key Points
content: compile (default): available everywhere, included in final artifact
test: only during test compile + run, NOT in final artifact — use for JUnit, Mockito, H2
runtime: not needed at compile time, included at runtime — JDBC drivers, logging implementations
provided: compile-time only, NOT in artifact, provided by container — servlet-api in WAR deployments
Wrong scope = classpath bloat or runtime ClassNotFoundException

sections.hook: Not every dependency belongs on the classpath at all times. Maven scopes let you say exactly when a library is needed — compile, test, or runtime.

beats.label: Classic examples:
items: Spring Boot starters → compile (always needed)
JUnit, Mockito, H2 → test (never in prod JAR)
JDBC driver → runtime (code compiles against java.sql interface, not the driver)
servlet-api in a WAR → provided (Tomcat supplies it at runtime)

beats.content: candidates miss: putting JUnit in compile scope doesn't break the build, but it bloats the artifact and leaks test infrastructure into prod. Always give test deps their correct scope. Wrong scope leads to either a fat artifact or a runtime ClassNotFoundException.

sections.cap: Scope is about intent. It tells Maven and your teammates exactly when a dependency is relevant — and keeps the final artifact lean.

questions.question: What are transitive dependencies in Maven and why can they cause problems?
questions.title: Transitive Dependencies in Maven
questions.direct_answer: Transitive dependencies are dependencies of your dependencies — Maven automatically pulls them in, but they can cause version conflicts when two libraries depend on different versions of the same artifact.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of dependency resolution complexity — this is where real-world Maven experience shows
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing what a transitive dependency is — thinking you only have the deps you explicitly declared
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Maven's nearest-wins conflict resolution strategy and how to override with explicit version declarations

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When you add Spring Boot Web to your project, you don't just get that library — you get all of its dependencies too, and their dependencies, and so on. These indirect dependencies are called transitive dependencies. Maven resolves the full dependency graph automatically, which is incredibly convenient. The problem arises when you have a diamond dependency scenario: your project depends on Library A and Library B, and both Library A and Library B depend on Jackson, but different versions. Library A needs Jackson 2.13, Library B needs Jackson 2.15. You can't have two versions of the same JAR on the classpath. Maven resolves this with the 'nearest wins' strategy — the version closest to your project in the dependency tree wins. This can lead to subtle bugs where the resolved version doesn't satisfy one of the libraries. The tool to diagnose this is 'mvn dependency:tree' which shows the full hierarchy of all dependencies including transitive ones, and you can see where version conflicts occur. To fix a conflict, you explicitly declare the desired version in your pom.xml dependencies — your direct declaration wins over any transitive version.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Transitive dependencies: dependencies of your dependencies — Maven pulls them all automatically
Version conflict: two deps require different versions of the same library
Maven resolution strategy: 'nearest wins' — closest to your pom.xml in dependency tree wins
'mvn dependency:tree': visualize full transitive dependency tree and spot conflicts
Fix conflicts: explicitly declare the desired version in your own pom.xml <dependencies>

sections.hook: You declare five dependencies in pom.xml but Maven downloads fifty. Those extras are transitive deps — and they're where version conflicts hide.

beats.content: A transitive dependency is a dependency of a dependency. Add Spring Boot Web and you also get Jackson, Tomcat, Hibernate Validator, and dozens more. Maven resolves the entire graph automatically. That's the good news.

The problem: Library A needs Jackson 2.13, Library B needs Jackson 2.15. You can't have two Jacksons on the classpath. Maven picks one using the nearest-wins rule — whichever version is closest to your pom.xml in the dependency tree wins. The other library might break silently.
production trap: NoSuchMethodError or ClassNotFoundException at runtime, even though the build compiled fine. Classic symptom of a transitive version conflict. Run mvn dependency:tree to find it.

beats.label: Fix strategy:
items: Run mvn dependency:tree to see which version won and who brought conflicting versions
Declare the desired version explicitly in your own pom.xml dependencies block
Your direct declaration always beats any transitive version

sections.cap: Transitive resolution is a superpower until you get a version conflict. Know the nearest-wins rule and keep mvn dependency:tree in your back pocket.

questions.question: How do you exclude a specific transitive dependency in Maven?
questions.title: Excluding Transitive Dependencies
questions.direct_answer: Use the <exclusions> element inside a dependency declaration to exclude specific transitive dependencies — useful when you want to replace a transitive dep with a different implementation or resolve version conflicts.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Maven troubleshooting skill — exclusions are occasionally needed in real projects
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing about exclusions and instead letting conflicting deps coexist — leads to runtime ClassNotFoundException
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a real-world example: excluding commons-logging from spring-core because you're using SLF4J instead

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Sometimes you need a dependency but don't want one of its transitive dependencies — either because you're providing a different implementation, because there's a security vulnerability in that transitive dep, or to resolve a version conflict. Maven's exclusion mechanism handles this. In the <dependency> block for the library that brings in the unwanted transitive dep, you add an <exclusions> block with an <exclusion> specifying the groupId and artifactId to exclude. For example, spring-core pulls in commons-logging as a transitive dependency. Many Spring projects exclude it and use SLF4J instead: inside the spring-core dependency declaration, you add an exclusion for commons-logging. Now Maven won't pull in commons-logging via that path. A practical tip: run 'mvn dependency:tree' first to identify exactly which dependency is bringing in the unwanted transitive dep, then add the exclusion to that specific parent dependency. Exclude by the most direct parent of the unwanted dep to be precise.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Add <exclusions><exclusion> inside a <dependency> to exclude its transitive deps
Exclusion needs: <groupId> and <artifactId> (wildcard * supported in Maven 3.2.1+)
Common use case: exclude commons-logging in favor of SLF4J, exclude old jackson versions
Run 'mvn dependency:tree' first to find which dependency brings in the unwanted transitive dep
After exclusion, you typically add the replacement library as a direct dependency

sections.hook: Sometimes a dependency drags in a transitive library you don't want. Maven's exclusion mechanism lets you surgically remove it.

beats.content: Inside the problematic dependency's block in pom.xml, add an exclusions element. Specify the groupId and artifactId of the transitive dep you want dropped. Maven will skip it when resolving that dependency's graph.

Classic example: spring-core pulls in commons-logging. Most Spring projects switch to SLF4J. So you add an exclusion for commons-logging inside the spring-core dependency block, then declare SLF4J as a direct dependency. Clean swap.

beats.label: Three-step workflow:
items: Run mvn dependency:tree to find which direct dep brings in the unwanted transitive dep
Add exclusion inside that direct dep's block
Add the replacement library as your own direct dependency

beats.content: sharp edge: Maven 3.2.1+ supports wildcard exclusion (*:*) which excludes all transitive deps of a library. Use it carefully — it's a blunt instrument and can drop things you actually need.

sections.cap: Exclusions are a targeted fix, not a first resort. Always run dependency:tree first to understand what you're removing and why.

questions.question: What is a BOM (Bill of Materials) in Maven and how does Spring Boot use it?
questions.title: Maven BOM (Bill of Materials)
questions.direct_answer: A BOM is a special POM that declares a curated set of dependency versions — importing a BOM lets you use those dependencies without specifying versions, trusting the BOM author to manage compatibility.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of advanced Maven dependency management — BOMs are used throughout the Spring ecosystem
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing BOM import (via dependencyManagement) with a regular dependency
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that spring-boot-starter-parent already provides a BOM — so most Spring Boot devs use it implicitly without knowing the BOM terminology

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A BOM — Bill of Materials — is a special Maven POM file that contains a <dependencyManagement> section listing a set of dependencies with their versions. When you import a BOM into your project, you're saying: 'I trust this BOM to define compatible versions for all these libraries.' The Spring Boot BOM, for example, lists compatible versions for Jackson, Hibernate, Tomcat, Netty, and dozens of other libraries. When you add those libraries to your dependencies section without a version, Maven looks them up in the BOM. A BOM is imported in your <dependencyManagement> section with scope 'import' and type 'pom'. This is different from a regular dependency — importing a BOM doesn't add it to your classpath, it just provides version information. Most Spring Boot developers use the spring-boot-starter-parent as a parent POM, which under the hood includes the Spring Boot BOM. But if your company has its own parent POM and you can't change the parent, you can still get Spring Boot's version management by importing the spring-boot-dependencies BOM via dependencyManagement.

sections.title: Key Points
content: BOM: a POM that declares curated compatible dependency versions — no code, just version info
Import a BOM via <dependencyManagement> with scope=import and type=pom
After BOM import: use managed dependencies without version tags
Spring Boot's BOM (spring-boot-dependencies) ensures all included libraries are compatible
spring-boot-starter-parent includes the BOM — most devs get BOM benefits implicitly through the parent

sections.hook: A BOM is basically a compatibility certificate for a group of libraries. Import it once and stop worrying about which versions work together.

beats.content: BOM stands for Bill of Materials. It's a special POM file that contains only a dependencyManagement section — no code, no real dependencies. It's a curated list of libraries and the versions that their authors have tested together.

You import a BOM in your own dependencyManagement block using scope=import and type=pom. After that, you can declare any of those libraries in your dependencies section without specifying a version. Maven resolves the version from the BOM.
Spring Boot's BOM (spring-boot-dependencies) covers Jackson, Hibernate, Tomcat, Netty, and hundreds of others. Spring's team tests these together so you get a guaranteed-compatible set.

non-obvious: if you use spring-boot-starter-parent as your parent POM, you're already getting the BOM for free — the parent includes it. The BOM import syntax is only needed when your project already has a corporate parent POM and can't change it.

sections.cap: A BOM gives you version management without a parent POM. Spring Boot uses it to guarantee that all its managed libraries play together, so you declare deps without worrying about versions.

questions.question: What does 'mvn dependency:tree' show and when do you use it?
questions.title: mvn dependency:tree
questions.direct_answer: 'mvn dependency:tree' displays the full hierarchical tree of all dependencies — both direct and transitive — helping you diagnose version conflicts, find which library pulls in an unwanted dependency, and understand your full classpath.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical diagnostic tooling knowledge — this is the first command experienced Maven developers run when debugging dependency issues
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing this command exists and manually searching pom.xml trying to understand why a certain version is being used
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention 'mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=groupId:artifactId' to filter the tree for a specific dependency

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: mvn dependency:tree is one of the most practically useful Maven commands to know. It prints your entire dependency graph as an indented tree. At the top level are your direct dependencies — the ones you've explicitly declared in pom.xml. Under each of those, indented, are their transitive dependencies, and their dependencies, and so on. The output also shows the scope of each dependency. I use this command in a few situations. First, when I see a ClassNotFoundException or NoSuchMethodError at runtime and I suspect a version conflict — I run dependency:tree to see what versions are being resolved for the conflicting library. Second, when I want to understand why a certain unexpected library is on my classpath — I can trace back through the tree to see which dependency brought it in. Third, when I need to add an exclusion — I need to know which direct dependency is the 'parent' of the transitive dep I want to exclude. You can filter the output: 'mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-core' shows only paths to Jackson in your tree.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Shows full dependency hierarchy: direct deps + all transitive deps
Use case 1: diagnose version conflicts causing ClassNotFoundException
Use case 2: find which library pulls in an unwanted transitive dependency
Use case 3: verify which version of a library is actually being used
Filter: '-Dincludes=groupId:artifactId' to search for a specific dependency in the tree

sections.hook: mvn dependency:tree is the first command to reach for when your build misbehaves at runtime. It shows you the full picture of everything on your classpath.

beats.content: This command prints your entire dependency graph as an indented tree. Your direct deps are at the top level. Under each one, indented, are their transitive deps, and so on. Each line shows the scope and whether a version was omitted because another version won the conflict.

beats.label: Three situations where it's essential:
items: ClassNotFoundException or NoSuchMethodError at runtime — version conflict, find it in the tree
Mystery library on your classpath — trace back which dep pulled it in
Before adding an exclusion — confirm which direct dep is the parent of the unwanted transitive dep

beats.content: Filtering is handy: mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-core shows only paths through the tree that involve Jackson. Much faster than reading the whole output.

candidates miss: the tree output marks omitted versions with (omitted for conflict) or (omitted for duplicate). That annotation is the exact line that tells you a version conflict was resolved and which version lost.

sections.cap: Treat mvn dependency:tree as your classpath X-ray. Any time something unexpectedly appears — or disappears — at runtime, this command is the first diagnostic step.
